newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israelis flock to Rabin murder site one year later.
newsitem.headline: Israelis flock to Rabin murder site one year later.

text.p: More than 100,000 Israelis returned on Saturday to the plaza where Yitzhak Rabin was assassinated to mark the year anniversary since the warrior turned peacemaker was felled by a right-wing Jewish gunman.

A 13-storey high projection of the slain prime minister smiled down on the many young people holding quiet vigil, dripping wax from memorial candles onto the square renamed in Rabin's honour after he was shot dead at a peace rally last November 4.
Police sources put the crowd at between 100,000 and 150,000.
The sombre, tearful atmosphere stood in sharp contrast to last year's joyful rally when supporters jubilantly celebrated Rabin's landmark peace deals with the Palestinians.
Rabin's gravelly voice opened the rally with the fateful echo of his last public speech:
"I believe there is a chance for peace. Your presence here proves that the people really want peace and oppose violence. Violence erodes Israeli society. We must condemn it."

Shortly after uttering those words, Rabin was shot dead by right-wing religious gunman Yigal Amir, who branded the former war hero a traitor for handing to the Palestinians West Bank land Amir viewed as promised the Jews by God.
Rabin's widow Leah on Saturday called on Israelis to continue the process Rabin began.
"I call on you to pick up the torch that Yitzhak carried and continue to spin the wheels of peace forward. Do not give up on peace because that was his testament," she told the crowd.

"The candles faded and the flowers wilted. Only the feeling of loss remains...but there is no alternative to your path. It will continue to be paved without you. People will continue to walk that path without you," she addressed her late husband.

Signs in the crowd reflected the bitterness felt by left-wing Israelis as Middle East peace moves have ground to a halt under right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who defeated Rabin successor Shimon Peres in May elections.
"We will not forget and we will not forgive!" said one sign.
"Rabin, only peace will avenge your blood," read another.
Many Israelis on the left accuse Netanyahu, who vigorously opposed Rabin's peace deals while in opposition, of helping create the atmosphere of political violence that precipitated the murder.
For many participants at Saturday's rally, the wound of the assassination had not yet healed.

"I was watching television when he was assassinated. They broke in with the report about the murder. I haven't stopped thinking about that since then. That's why I came tonight," 22-year-old Tzvi Kessler told Reuters.
One woman expressed doubt that the assassination had mellowed Israel's often harsh political culture.
"I feel this thing was forgotten too quickly," said Shlomit Shauli, 30. "Maybe people here learned a lesson but the people who incited are still inciting and the murderers are running free."

In the West Bank village of Husan earlier on Saturday, hundreds of Palestinians were joined by a handful of leftist Israeli leaders to mourn the killing of an 11-year Palestinian boy by a Jewish settler this week.
Nahum Kurman, security chief of Hadar Beitar settlement in the West Bank was charged on Friday with manslaughter after hitting Hilmi Shousha on the head with the butt of his pistol, killing the boy.
"I see a growth of violence...inside the Jewish community, This child was murdered...this child is a victim for nothing," left-wing Israeli lawmaker Yael Dayan said at the Husan memorial.
"I have pain but I still have hope," she added.
